text: The Roman god Mithras took his name from Mithra, an old god of Iran.
At Mount Nemrut, a king set up giant statues where Mithras sat among the gods.
src: The Roman Mithras takes his name from Mithra, an old pre-Zoroastrian and later Zoroastrian god of Iran
King Antiochus I of Commagene set up colossal statues at Mount Nemrut in which Mithras, beardless and in Parthian dress, sat among the gods

text: More than 1,900 years ago, the worship of Mithras began in the Roman Empire, probably centred in Rome.
Scholars still argue about how much of it came from Persia.
src: the Roman Empire, where its earliest temples appear in the last quarter of the 1st century CE, apparently with its centre in Rome
how much else came from Persia is debated

text: Every temple had a picture of Mithras killing a bull, looking back towards the sun god Sol.
Followers met for shared meals in small temples underground, made to look like a cave.
src: At the heart of every temple was the image of Mithras killing a bull, the tauroctony / looking back towards the sun god Sol
met for ritual meals in small underground temples, the mithraea, made to represent the cave where Mithras killed the bull

text: Many followers were soldiers, and the religion spread along the Rhine and Danube rivers and to Britain.
Followers passed through seven grades, or steps, and joined by shaking hands with their leader.
src: Soldiers were strongly represented / the cult spread through Rome and Ostia, the Rhine and Danube frontiers, North Africa and Britain
passed through seven grades / admission ended with a handshake with the pater

text: More than 1,600 years ago, Christians persecuted its followers, and the religion came to an end.
What remains are its temples, carvings, writing on temple walls and a few scraps of papyrus.
src: In the 4th century Mithraists faced persecution from Christians, and the religion ended between that century’s last decade and the 5th century
About 420 sites have yielded remains / the main Mithraic texts are the graffiti on temple walls and the inscriptions on monuments / a fragment of a catechism for the Lion grade on an Egyptian papyrus
